title: Get By Anywhere — Module 1: 30-Day Crash Course
note: One phrase a day. Written once in English. The page shows the left column in the learner's language and the right column in the language they are learning. The teammate teaches it by voice. v2: numbers on days 8 and 11 (split); 'How far' folded into directions; day 28 is one phrase; culture tips added.

buildup: Hello, good morning. How are you?
days.use: The first word out of your mouth, every time. A greeting before a question changes how people treat you.
days.formality: Learn the polite version first; it works with everyone.
days.culture: In France, Italy, Spain, and Japan, greet the shopkeeper or waiter the moment you walk in. Not doing it reads as rude.

days.use: Ends almost every request. 'Thank you' is the most-used phrase of your whole trip.
days.formality: Always safe. Overuse it; nobody minds.
days.culture: In Japan and Korea a small bow goes with thank you. In France 'merci' alone can sound curt — add 'monsieur' or 'madame'.

days.use: Answering the questions people ask you: Table by the window? Sparkling? Bag?

buildup: Excuse me, may I ask you something?
days.use: To get a waiter's or a stranger's attention before you ask anything.
days.formality: Use the polite form with strangers.
days.culture: In Japan, one word does the job of both 'excuse me' and 'sorry' — your teammate will explain which words your language uses.

days.use: Bumping into someone, stepping in the wrong line, spilling a coffee.
days.formality: Many languages use a different word for 'sorry' (apology) than for 'excuse me' (attention). Your teammate will tell you if yours does.

buildup: Excuse me, do you speak English?
days.use: Ask this BEFORE launching into English. People help more when you asked first.
days.culture: Asking this first, in their language, is the single most respectful thing a traveler can do — even if you then switch to English.

buildup: I'm sorry, I don't understand. Slowly, please?
days.use: Buys you time and kindness. Then open the translator.

buildup: A table for two. Three tickets. Five euros.
days.use: Prices, tickets, tables, floors. You'll hear numbers before you say any other new phrase — learn them first.
days.reply: (Practice: your teammate says a number in words — you say the next one.)

buildup: Excuse me, where is the bathroom?
days.use: The question everyone needs. 'Where is' is the pattern for the next three days.
days.formality: Polite form. Some countries say 'toilet', some say 'restroom' — your teammate picks the local word.

buildup: Excuse me, where is the train station?
days.use: Same pattern as yesterday with a new noun. Swap in 'bus stop', 'airport', 'hotel'.

buildup: Ten euros. Eight o'clock. Room seven.
days.use: Finishes the set. From now on the prices and times in the replies are yours.
days.reply: (Practice: your teammate says a price, you repeat it.)

buildup: Turn left, then straight ahead. It's not far.
days.use: You'll HEAR these more than say them — they're the answer to yesterday's question. 'Is it far?' decides between walking and a taxi.
Train or bus counter. Say the city name the local way if you can.

buildup: Is this the bus to the airport?
days.use: Ask the driver before you get on. Saves an hour going the wrong way.
Taxi. Also 'the next stop, please' on a bus.
days.culture: In Italy and Spain, dinner starts late — eight or nine o'clock. Show up at six and the kitchen is closed.

buildup: Good evening. A table for two, please.
days.use: Walking into a restaurant. Change the number as needed.

buildup: The menu, please. In English, if you have it.
days.use: If there's no English menu, the photo translator reads it for you.

buildup: I would like the pasta, please
days.use: Ordering. Point at the menu and say this — it works even if you can't pronounce the dish.
days.formality: 'I would like' is more polite than 'I want' in most languages.

days.use: Yesterday's reply was 'And to drink?' — this is your answer.
days.culture: In much of Europe the check never comes until you ask. In Japan you usually pay at the register, not at the table.

days.use: In many countries the waiter will NOT bring it until you ask.
days.formality: Polite form. Your teammate will use the local word — 'bill' or 'check'.
days.culture: In markets, a smile and a slight pause after the price is normal. In shops, the price is the price.

days.use: Markets, taxis, anything without a price tag.
days.culture: Small cafés and market stalls in many countries are cash only. Ask before you order.

days.use: Ask BEFORE you order in small places.
days.culture: In many countries the hotel keeps your passport for a few minutes at check-in. That's normal.

buildup: Hello, I have a reservation. My name is ___.
days.use: Hotel front desk and restaurants you booked ahead.
days.culture: Ask if breakfast is included. In Japan, 'breakfast' may mean rice and fish, not toast.

buildup: What time is breakfast, and where?
days.use: Also works for 'What time is checkout?' and 'What time does it open?'

buildup: Excuse me, can you help me, please?
days.use: Lost, confused, or the machine ate your ticket. Then open the translator.
days.reply: Of course. What do you need?

buildup: I'm looking for a pharmacy. Is there one nearby?
days.use: Pharmacy, ATM, supermarket, my hotel. Swap the noun.

days.phrase: Do you have this in a smaller size?
buildup: Do you have this in a smaller size?
Do you have this in another color?
days.use: Shopping. Same pattern for 'bigger', 'another color', 'in blue'.

buildup: I need a doctor. It's urgent.
days.use: Say it first, then open the translator for the details.
days.formality: Neutral. Learn it so well you can say it when you're scared.

buildup: Call the police, please. My bag was stolen.
days.use: Also learn the local emergency number — your teammate knows it.

buildup: Nice to meet you. Goodbye, and thank you!
days.use: The last thing they hear from you. End every exchange with it.
days.culture: In France and Italy, saying goodbye when you leave a shop is as expected as hello when you enter.
